newsitem.title: USA: Thai economy plan good, but snags loom-US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy plan good, but snags loom-US analysts.

text.p: Thailand took the proper first steps toward rejuvenating its economy on Tuesday, U.S. investors and analysts said.
But some analysts warned the $12.0 to $15.0 billion bailout package may be too small, while the austerity measures it would require may be severe enough to generate substantial domestic opposition.
Earlier, the Thai government unveiled economic measures recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as prerequisites for the loans the country seeks.

To secure the loans from the IMF and foreign nations, the government proposed the suspension of 42 of the country's 91 finance firms. It also pledged to boost foreign reserves, balance the budget, trim inflation and cut the current account deficit.
One measure expected to draw strong domestic opposition was an increase in the value added tax (VAT) to 10 percent from seven percent.

"These are the right steps," said Joyce Chang, emerging markets debt strategist at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc. "The package had a lot of things in it that the market expected, that are typical for an IMF package."

For the economic rescue plan to work, it must provide enough liquidity to cover the credit crunch in the country's corporate sector, where about $38.0 billion of debt falls due in the coming year, Chang said.
Investors would remain concerned over whether the $12.0 billion to $15.0 billion in loans would pay all the bills, she said.

Mike Rosborough, a portfolio manager at PIMCO, said the requested aid package would likely restore investor confidence in the sagging baht. A rebound in the currency would allow Thailand to draw less heavily on the loans, he said.
"If it restores confidence and the baht begins to stabilize and interest rates begin to fall, you may have to draw on less than (the proposed amount)," he said. "I think it's probably enough."
The proposed economic measures would likely slow Thailand's Gross Ddomestic Product (GDP) growth to annual rates not seen in more than a decade, Chang said.
While the country's economy should continue to expand, growth would be closer to 3.0 or 4.0 percent than the 9.0 to 10.0 percent of recent years, she added.
Convincing the Thai government and people to swallow such a bitter pill could be difficult, a New York-based broker of Thai stocks said.
"Everybody's looking at the economic impact and trying to add the numbers up. Nobody's looking at the social impact," the broker said.
State-enterprise unions and certain cabinet members were likely to oppose the economic reform package put forth by Thailand's finance minister and central bank president, he said.
In particular, unions may protest finance minister Thanong Bidaya's goal of speeding privatization, the broker said.
"The state-enterprise unions in Thailand tend to be very militant," he said.
But PIMCO's Rosborough said Thailand would likely adhere to the IMF's recommendations.
"I guess the question is, what alternative do they have? Regardless of whether they like it, they'll accept it," Rosborough said.
(( -- Emerging Markets Unit, 212-859-1868 ))
